job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Uma Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My days are organised, because I make lists or I panic. I wake up in the box room of a three-bed house in Millbrook that I share with two flatmates, check the job boards, and tailor two applications properly rather than blast out twenty. I studied economics, did six weeks in the finance office at Larkfield Homes Trust, a housing charity, and now I work fifteen hours a week at a pharmacy counter. My dad drives a taxi back home and he can't help with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To be fair, I'd say it's a relief that the hype is overblown, though I'd stay cautious. At work I'd mention the small time-savers, like summarising long reports, which I already do now and then. With friends I'd say prices and rent are the real story, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing in my life gets easier. Rent in Millbrook has gone up twice since I moved in, and my loan has interest that grows faster than my pharmacy wage. A job that pays twenty-eight thousand would fix a lot, but there are maybe four finance openings in the whole county.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen the search to the next city, which is forty minutes by train, and count the fare against the pay. I'd ask Larkfield for a reference and a coffee with their finance manager. I'd also keep the pharmacy hours and put two hundred a month aside before spending anything on myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit heavy, to be fair. I'm not panicking, because I can see a path, but my mum asks every Sunday whether I've heard anything. Those calls make my chest tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the coffee with the finance manager at Larkfield actually be for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn how the charity hires. They're a small team, and the manager told me posts often go to people they already know from placements. If I stay in touch, I could be the name that comes to mind when somebody leaves. It's slow, but it's honest and I know she liked my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the two hundred a month come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the pharmacy wage minus rent, which leaves me about three hundred. I'd stop buying lunches out and walk instead of taking the bus. Two hundred sounds brave, but it would mean a cushion of one month's expenses by Christmas, which I don't have today.

say: I'd say the **hype** is overblown but stay cautious about it.
With friends I'd say **rent and prices** are the real story.
think: Nothing gets easier: rent rose twice and **loan interest** outruns my pharmacy wage.
There are maybe **four finance openings** in the whole county.
do: Widen the search to the **next city**, forty minutes away by train.
Ask Larkfield for a **reference** and a coffee with their finance manager.
feel: A **heavy** feeling, but not panic, because there is a path.

Her anxiety comes from rent, debt and few local openings, not from technology.

steps.text: Apply for finance jobs in the city forty minutes away by train
Ask Larkfield for a reference and a coffee with their manager
Put two hundred a month aside before spending on anything else
Keep the fifteen pharmacy hours a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and the policy has to catch up. At the charity that took me on for six weeks, I'd say we need clear rules on how firms use these tools and who is responsible when software gets numbers wrong. Online I'd share good reporting on this and ignore the shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first jobs to shrink are the ones I want: reconciling accounts, checking invoices, preparing basic reports. I've seen at Larkfield how a spreadsheet tool did in an hour what the junior did in a day. So employers will hire fewer juniors and expect them to supervise software. That scares me, but I also think I can do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the AI tools seriously, not just now and then. I'd do an evening course on data and accounting software that I could add to my CV by spring. I'd keep applying, but to roles that mention analysis and checking AI output, not just data entry, and I'd join a graduate group on the finance union's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a bit of fire. I'd rather be the person who knows how to check the machine than one it replaces. Still, it's heavy knowing the employers choose how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does checking the machine look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I imagine reading what the software produced, spotting a wrong figure or a missing invoice, and explaining it to a manager in plain words. It's the same accuracy I was trained for, only with a different first draft. The hard part is that firms may decide one reviewer can cover what ten juniors did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should carry the cost of all this change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not graduates. If firms save money by not hiring juniors, they should pay into training funds, the way they pay for health and safety. I'd vote for anyone who makes that a rule rather than a promise.

I'd share good reporting and **ignore** the shouting.
think: The jobs I want, like **reconciling accounts**, shrink first.
I'd rather be the person who **checks the machine** than the one replaced.
do: Take an **evening course** on data and accounting software by spring.
Apply for roles that mention **analysis** and checking AI output.
Join a graduate group run by a **finance union**.
feel: **Worried**, with a bit of fire: knowing employers choose how this goes.

fieldNote: She turns worry into a skills plan, which fits her steady, proven-first approach.
Insists employers, not graduates, should carry the **cost** of change.
Her Larkfield internship gives her a concrete picture of what software already does.

steps.text: Finish an evening course in data and accounting software by spring
Use AI tools weekly to check figures in practice tasks
Apply for analyst and audit-support roles, not only data entry
Join the finance union's graduate group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an emergency for people my age and ask for rules and public support. Two years is too short for firms or governments to prepare. I'd sign any petition for retraining funds and a basic safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the whole finance route is gone by the time I'm 25. A degree in economics assumes there will be analysis work for people to do, and that's exactly what the machines do best. With my debt and no cushion, I'd be in trouble quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any paid job now, including more pharmacy hours, and put every spare pound into a rainy-day account. I'd also call my parents and tell them honestly where I am, and ask whether I could move back to the taxi flat for a year if things collapse. And I'd get involved with local groups pushing for retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry at how little notice there is. I keep thinking of my dad, who has driven the same taxi for years and might be replaced too. We'd all be scrambling together, which is strange comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you go back to your parents' flat if you could stay in Millbrook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rent is the bill I can't shrink. A room costs me four hundred and forty a month, and without graduate pay I couldn't carry it. Moving home would hurt my pride, but it would give me time to retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2031. Does that change anything for the pharmacy counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The pharmacy already uses a dispensing robot in the back, so the counter staff matter less each year. I'd treat those hours as a bridge for maybe three years. After that, I think hands-on jobs also stop being a safe backup, and it's one reason I'd want government help early.

say: I'd call it an **emergency** and ask for retraining funds and a safety net.
I'd sign every **petition** for public support.
think: The whole **finance route** could be gone by the time I'm 25.
With debt and no cushion, I'd be in **trouble** quickly.
do: Take every **pharmacy hour** I can and save every spare pound.
Ask my parents if I can **move home** for a year if things collapse.
Join local groups pushing for **retraining** money.
feel: **Frightened** and angry about how little notice there is.
S2.quote: Moving home would hurt my pride, but it would give me time to retrain.
fieldNote: Ready to put pride aside and move back to the family home if needed.

steps.text: Take every extra pharmacy counter shift offered
Put every spare pound into a rainy-day account
Ask parents about moving home for a year if work dries up
Join a local group campaigning for retraining money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives time to make rules and for people to retrain. I'd say governments must start a retraining fund this year, not in year four. I'd also tell people who are younger than me to keep options open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd get maybe two or three years in a finance job before things change a lot. That's enough to pay off a good part of my loan and build a skill I can carry. It's not a safe plan, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job this year, even if it's not ideal, and treat it as a training ground. I'd learn the AI tools properly and look for where people still check, explain and decide. I'd put away three hundred a month and look at a master's in data or public policy, funded by work if possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously hopeful. Five years feels like enough to jump rather than fall. Still, I don't want to be naive, and I get a flutter in my stomach when I picture 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first job that you wouldn't do with only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd actually invest in it. I'd ask for tasks beyond data entry, learn the client side and take professional exams. With two years, I'd just grab cash and save, but with five I can build something that carries over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why public policy as a possible master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to decide how this change is handled, and my economics background fits. I'd also like to feel I'm helping fix the problem, not only surviving it. It's a long shot, but it matches what I care about.

I'd tell younger people to keep **options** open.
think: I'd get maybe **two or three years** in a finance job before things change a lot.
That is enough to pay off part of my **loan**.

fieldNote: Longer warning turns her plan from survival into building something.

steps.text: Take the first finance job offered and ask for tasks beyond data entry
Learn the AI tools properly through the employer's training
Save three hundred a month toward a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means we can do this properly. I'd say schools, universities and employers should rebuild how people learn and what a graduate is for. I'd be calm in public and also quietly active.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel relatively safe. In ten years I could be in a good career, debt-free and financially steady, and maybe in a role where people still need me, like advising or auditing. The risk is being a mid-level person when everything shifts, so I'd have to keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with a normal first job, pay down the loan, and use the first two years to learn how a finance team works. Then I'd study at night for a recognised qualification and look at moving into a role that explains numbers to people. I'd also vote and volunteer for groups that push for fair rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. There's still a knot of worry because I don't know what I'll be at thirty-three, but it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your younger cousins to do with a ten-year warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to choose work that mixes people and judgement, and learn how to use the tools without being scared. I'd also say not to take on debt until the degree has a clear path to a job. I wish someone had told me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about the next year, if you knew you had ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry less about every single application and more about being useful somewhere. A steady job, a small savings habit and a course that adds something real. Panic gets me nowhere, and I know that from this autumn.

I'd stay calm in public and **quietly active**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because I don't have savings or a safety net, and two years isn't enough for the system to adjust. What would help is a public training fund, an entry job guarantee, and some breathing room on my loan payments while I get settled.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that young people aren't asking to be rescued. Panic gets me nowhere, and I know that from this autumn. We just want a fair route in while the ground is moving.

headlineQuote: Panic gets me nowhere, and I know that from this autumn.
portrait: Uma, 23, has a **good economics degree**, six weeks at a housing charity and fifteen pharmacy hours, sharing a rented house.
She is organised, makes lists, and uses AI **now and then**, which helps her turn worry into a plan.
She blames firms that cut training, and wants **clear rules** and a public safety net.
Her mood is anxious in most worlds because rent, loan interest and few local openings are already heavy.
With ten years, she feels **steadier**, and would study at night and push for fair rules.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, with no savings and too little time for the system to adjust.
whatWouldHelp: A public **training fund**, an entry job guarantee, and breathing room on **loan payments**.
